item.title: Optimal self-orthogonal binary linear codes
item.description: We complete the determination of the minimum possible length of eight-dimensional binary self-orthogonal codes with given minimum distance. For dimension nine we give exact values and bounds for minimum distance at most $64$. By exploiting the geometric reformulation of linear codes as multisets of points, we fully redo the classification for dimension at most seven in a simplified and computer-free manner. As a by-product we prove the non-existence of $[93,9,44]_2$ codes and show several divisibility results for putative optimal nine-dimensional binary codes.

item.title: Local Convergence of Triadic Closures of Sparse Random Graphs
item.description: Triadic closure is a natural mechanism for modeling the clustering phenomenon observed in many real-world networks. Given a possibly random undirected graph $H$, we consider pairs of non-adjacent vertices that have a common neighbor. Conditional on $H$, each such pair is joined by an edge independently and simultaneously, with a probability depending on the degrees of its endpoints and on the number of their common neighbors. The resulting graph is called a triadic closure of $H$. We study the effect of this operation on local convergence. More precisely, we prove that if a sequence of potentially random finite undirected graphs of $\left( H_n \right)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ converges locally in probability to a rooted graph $H^*$, then the corresponding sequence of triadic closures converges locally in probability to the same triadic closure of $H^*$. As a consequence, we obtain a general limit theorem for the clustering coefficients of triadic closures. In particular, we show that the triadic closures can have a strictly positive limiting clustering coefficients even when the limiting clustering coefficients of the parent graph sequence is zero. Finally, we apply our results to several classical sparse random graph models including Erdős-Rényi, configuration, preferential attachment models and compute the limiting clustering coefficients of their triadic closures.

item.title: Diameter-two graphs whose mutual-visibility chromatic number equals their chromatic number
item.description: A set $S$ of vertices of a graph $G$ is a mutual-visibility set if every pair of vertices of $S$ is joined by a shortest path whose internal vertices avoid $S$, and the mutual-visibility chromatic number $χ_μ(G)$ is the least number of mutual-visibility sets into which $V(G)$ can be partitioned. Klavžar, Kuziak, Valenzuela Tripodoro and Yero (2025) proved that $χ_μ(G)\leχ(G)$ whenever $G$ has diameter two, observed that equality holds for complete bipartite graphs, and asked whether there are any other diameter-two graphs attaining equality. We answer this question in the affirmative. We construct a graph $G_{11}$ of order 11 and diameter two with $χ_μ(G_{11})=χ(G_{11})=3$, and an infinite family of such graphs obtained from $G_{11}$ by replacing one vertex with pairwise non-adjacent copies of it.

item.title: Moments of Magic Squares: Line-Sum Conditions, a Permutation Threshold, and Random Energies
item.description: Every semi-magic square of order $n$ satisfies the axial moment identities $\sum_{i,j}s_{ij}j^m=\sum_{i,j}s_{ij}i^m=M(n)\sum_jj^m$ for all $m\ge1$, where $M(n)=n(n^2+1)/2$. For real matrices the converse requires $1\le m\le n-1$, whereas for arrangements of $\{1,\dots,n^2\}$ fewer moments suffice once $n\ge14$. We define the permutation threshold $k^*(n)$ as the least $k$ such that every arrangement satisfying these identities for $1\le m\le k$ is semi-magic. In terms of the column-sum deviations $γ_j$, the degree-$k$ conditions state that $\sum_jγ_jt^j$ is divisible by $(t-1)^{k+1}$, linking $k^*(n)$ to the Prouhet--Tarry--Escott problem. While Schur's bound on real zeros gives $k^*(n)\le\sqrt{2(n-1)\log(n^4/4)}$, we prove the converse realisability bound $k^*(n)\ge(\sqrt2-o(1))\sqrt n$ (and $k^*(n)\ge(\sqrt6-o(1))\sqrt n$ when $4\mid n$) by perturbing semi-magic squares with complementary row pairs via horizontal swaps. We also show that $k^*(n)=n-1$ for $3\le n\le13$, $k^*(n)=n-2$ for $14\le n\le17$, and $k^*(n)\le n-3$ for $n\ge18$, and determine $k^*(n)$ for $18\le n\le40$ with computer assistance. Finally, at the $k=1$ level of the hierarchy, we specialise the Mantel--Hubert quadratic assignment variance formula to obtain exact means, variances, and limit laws under a uniform random arrangement for the full line-sum energy $E_{\mathrm{full}}$, for the four-term energy $E_4$ combining the first moments and the two diagonals, and for Loly's moment of inertia, and find that $|L_4|=14{,}639{,}440$ arrangements of order $4$ satisfy $E_4=0$.

item.title: Antimagic Labeling of Central Digraphs Constructed from Loops
item.description: Let $(T, \circ)$ be a loop of order $k \geq 3$ and $D_S^*$ the loopless central digraph obtained from the associated central digraph $D_S$ by removing the $k$ self-loops at the diagonal vertices. We construct an explicit arc-labeling $f$ of $D_S^*$ ordering all arcs lexicographically by $(\text{tail}, \text{head})$ and assigning labels $1, \ldots, m$ in that order and prove that $f$ is an antimagic labeling. Consequently, $D_S$ is antimagic for every loop of order $k \geq 3$, a property that depends only on $k$ and is invariant across all non-isomorphic loops of the same order.

item.title: Re-Ordering the Generalized Hofstadter Functions G, H, and Beyond
item.description: Hofstadter's G function is recursively defined via G(0) = 0 and then G(n) = n-G(G(n -1)). Following Hofstadter, we vary the number k of nested recursive calls in this equation and obtain a family of functions (F\_k). In a previous article, we proved that this family is ordered pointwise: for all k and n, we have $F_k(n) $le$ F_{k+1}(n)$. Here we propose a much shorter proof of this theorem, without infinite morphic words. The key ingredient for this direct proof is a new formula expressing iterates of the preimages of $F_k$ . Thanks to this formula, we also prove several conjectures mentioned in our previous article. In particular we obtain that $F_k(n) < F_{k+1}(n)$ when n > (k + 1)(k + 6)/2. We provide a certified formalization of all these results in the Rocq proof assistant.

item.title: Admissible sets of integers in imaginary quadratic fields of class number 1
item.description: Let $\mathcal O_K$ be the ring of integers of a number field $K$. A finite subset $\mathcal H=\{η_1,\ldots,η_k\}\subset\mathcal O_K$ is said to be \emph{admissible} if for every prime ideal $\mathfrak p$ in $\mathcal O_K$, the reductions of the $η_i$ modulo $\mathfrak p$ do not represent every residue class. The diameter of a finite subset $S$ of $\mathcal O_K$ is defined to be \[\mathrm{diam}(S):= \max_{η_i,η_j\in S:η_i\neqη_j}|\mathcal N(η_i-η_j)|\] where $\mathcal N$ denotes the norm down to the rational field. This paper computationally investigates admissible subsets of rings of integers in imaginary quadratic fields of class number 1 (such as the Gaussian integers or the Eisenstein integers) that are large relative to their diameter. The motivation is twofold. Firstly, there is the improvement of results analogous to the question of an upper bound for the least gap between large rational primes, which has been one of the great number theoretic successes of the twenty-first century. A second motivation is that there is the opportunity to disprove a variation of the second Hardy-Littlewood conjecture. The calculations in the paper provide new records on the smallest distance between primes in the fields in question, and explicit counter-examples to a generalisation of the second Hardy-Littlewood conjecture in all bar one of the fields.

item.title: Online Discrepancy of Sparse Random Vectors over Long Horizons
item.description: We study online vector balancing for independent sparse random vectors: each arrival is supported on a uniformly random set of $s$ of the $n$ coordinates, with nonzero entries equal to one (binary model) or independent random signs (signed model), and an online algorithm must sign each vector upon arrival. The prefix discrepancy is the largest $\ell_\infty$-norm of the signed sums up to the horizon $T$, the terminal discrepancy that of the sum at time $T$. For binary inputs with $2\le s\le n/2$ and $T=Θ(n)$, Altschuler and Tikhomirov showed that both are of order $\sqrt{s}+\log\log n$; they asked how the prefix discrepancy depends on the horizon and whether a matching terminal bound holds at every prescribed time. Over long horizons, the two differ. For every fixed $s\ge2$ and $c>0$, every online algorithm, even a randomized one that knows the horizon, incurs with high probability prefix discrepancy $Ω(\log\log n+(\log T/\log n)^{α_s})$ for $n\le T\le e^{cn}$, where $α_s=(2^{s-1}-1)/(2^s-1)$. For $s=2$, quadratic Greedy matches this bound; for fixed $s\ge3$, we give an online algorithm with prefix discrepancy $O(\log\log n+(\log T/\log n)^{1/2})$. In contrast, a deterministic algorithm that knows neither the horizon nor the failure probability keeps the terminal discrepancy $O_k(\sqrt{s}+\log\log n)$ at each prescribed time, with failure probability $n^{-k}$ for every fixed $k$, for $2\le s\le n/2$ (binary model) and $2\le s\le n$ (signed model); for $s=2$, quadratic Greedy itself does so. This answers their terminal question, and the same order is optimal for prefixes at all polynomial horizons $T\ge n$. The lower bound uses a finite safety game realized within the input law; the upper bounds use moments of elementary symmetric polynomials and, at terminal times, a $\cosh$ potential or a translated gauge with a Foster inequality at every state.

item.title: Logarithmic asymptotics for polynomial threshold functions
item.description: We count Boolean functions represented as the sign of a real polynomial of bounded degree on the $n$-dimensional cube. We prove that the logarithm of their number is asymptotic to that of the classical hyperplane-arrangement upper bound, uniformly over all degrees, with relative error $O((\log n)^2/n)$. We also obtain sharper additive and relative error estimates in particular degree ranges, including an additive error $O(n^2)$ between the logarithms throughout a small linear degree range and improved bounds just below the central degree. The proof combines probabilistic estimates for Reed--Muller codes with a deletion argument for sets of evaluation vectors, an entropy count, and a sharp-threshold estimate for expected rank deficiency.

item.title: A general algebraic characterization of extremal $Δ$-trees and $k$-cyclic graphs for degree-homogeneous VDB indices
item.description: We present a general algebraic method for maximizing a vertex-degree-based (VDB) topological index $TI(G) = \sum_{uv \in E(G)} f(d(u),d(v))$ over the class of $n$-vertex trees with a prescribed maximum degree $Δ\ge 3$. By expressing the edge multiplicities of the basis $\mathcal{B} = \{(1,Δ), (Δ,Δ)\}$ via degree-sum identities, we reduce the maximization of $TI(T)$ to the minimization of an explicit discrete penalty function $G(x,y)$ over the non-basic edges. We formulate five analytical conditions on the weight function $f(x,y)$ that dictate the optimal edge distributions, yielding a complete characterization of the extremal trees across all congruence classes of $n \pmod{Δ- 1}$. Additionally, we provide their explicit construction by attaching leaves to a core of internal vertices. Applying this framework, we obtain the complete characterization of extremal $Δ$-trees for the Degree-Ratio Sombor ($DRSO$), Symmetric Division Deg ($SDD$), and Hyperbolic Sombor ($HSO$) indices for all $Δ\ge 3$. Furthermore, the analytical conditions identify the exact degree thresholds for the Arithmetic-Geometric ($AG$) and Diminished Sombor ($DSO$) indices, showing that the same extremal family maximizes $AG$ if and only if $3 \le Δ\le 8$, and $DSO$ if and only if $3 \le Δ\le 4$. Finally, since changing the edge count from $m = n - 1$ to $m = n - 1 + k$ affects only the constant term in the decomposition while leaving the penalty function $G(x,y)$ invariant, the method extends directly to connected $k$-cyclic graphs.

item.title: Three Quadratic Recurrences Modulo 3: What We Can Prove and What We Can Guess
item.description: We study three innocent-looking recurrences modulo $3$, each built from squares of two earlier terms. One of them turns out to be secretly $\textit{linear}$, and we can compute its periods exactly. One is a $\textit{permutation}$ hiding a small, perfectly orderly piece inside a large, random-looking one. The third looks thoroughly random, but it still has a few provable features. Along the way we meet open problems that need nothing beyond a first course in abstract algebra to state. This paper is a starting point, not the final word in any sense.

item.title: Asymptotic Rank of Complete Graph Tensors
item.description: Graph tensors extend the matrix multiplication tensor by placing a two-party identity tensor on every edge of a graph and keeping one tensor leg at every vertex. We study the asymptotic rank of the tensor associated with the complete graph. For every integer $n\geq 2$, over the complex numbers, we prove \[ \left\lfloor\frac{n^2}{4}\right\rfloor \leq \log_2\widetilde R\bigl(\mathsf{GT}_2(K_n)\bigr) \leq \frac{n^2}{4}. \] The upper bound matches the maximum-cut lower bound for every even $n$ and differs from it by only $1/4$ for every odd $n$. In particular, the exponent per edge is below $2/3$ for every $n\geq5$, answering a question of Christandl, Vrana, and Zuiddam. Our proof extends the polynomial multiplication approach underlying OpenAI's bound $ω\leq9/4$. The main step separates any fixed number of shared tensor legs simultaneously, using only linearly many direct-sum copies in the number of blocks. This yields an entropy inequality for higher-order tensors. We apply it to the tensor for multiplying $n-1$ polynomials, whose rank is linear in the input length. Discrete concavity and a shifted tripling inequality then force a lower bound on a symmetrized spectral profile. Comparing this growth with polynomial interpolation gives the stated upper bound while preserving all $n$ tensor legs. We also prove an operational barrier for these higher-order polynomial constructions. For $n\geq3$, the specified formal reduction rules cannot certify an exponent below $n^2/4$ for $\mathsf{GT}_2(K_n)$, even after taking tensor powers and allowing subexponential overhead and common auxiliary factors. This extends the symmetric three-leg barrier of Amanov, van den Berg, and Zuiddam and explains the remaining gap for odd complete graphs within this method.

item.title: Extremal diagonal-coherent binary codes: shortened Hamming cores, deep holes, and the 64 I-Ching hexagrams
item.description: Each of the 64 hexagrams of the I-Ching, or Book of Changes, is a stack of six Yin-Yang lines and is therefore a binary vector of length 6; the eight hexagrams formed by repeating a single trigram span a doubled-trigram subspace $Δ$. We ask which binary $[6,3,3]$ codes are compatible with this trigram structure. We show that a $[6,3,3]$ code meets $Δ$ in at most four codewords, that the four are then forced to be the doubled trigrams Earth, Fire, Wind and Lake, and that exactly two codes attain this bound: the shortened Hamming code $\mathcal C_A$ and its dual. Since $\mathcal C_A$ has covering radius 2, its eight codewords, their radius-one balls, and its eight deep holes together reconstruct all 64 hexagrams. In general, we call a binary code of length $2m$ with $d \ge 3$ diagonal-coherent if it contains the half of the diagonal subspace $\{(u,u)\}$ coming from even-weight vectors $u$ -- the largest part of that subspace a single-error-correcting code can contain -- and extremal if its dimension is as large as possible. For $m\ge2$ and $r=\lceil\log_2(2m+1)\rceil$, we determine the number $N(m)$ of extremal diagonal-coherent codes with parameters $[\,2m,\ 2m-r,\ \ge3\,]$, show that diagonal coherence entails no loss of redundancy, and determine their minimum distances. We also put these codes in a normal form, determine their hulls, and show that each has covering radius $2$ with exactly $2^r-1-2m$ deep-hole cosets. Finally we propose three open problems.

item.title: A proof of Wang's planar D-coloring conjecture
item.description: We prove Wang's planar D-coloring conjecture. A D-coloring of a graph is a proper edge coloring in which every subgraph isomorphic to $K_4$ minus an edge is rainbow. Wang conjectured that every planar graph of maximum degree $Δ$ has a D-coloring with 9 colors if $Δ=4$, 10 colors if $Δ=5$, and $2Δ-1$ colors if $Δ\ge 6$. Hu, Kong and Wang proved the cases $Δ\le 5$ and $Δ\ge 33$. We prove the sharp bound $2Δ-1$ for every $Δ\ge 6$, settling the remaining cases. The proof uses discharging; the case $Δ=6$ is computer-assisted.

item.title: Subgraph Isomorphism, Integer Linear Programming, and Lattices: A Linear Algebraic Framework
item.description: The subgraph isomorphism problem (SGI) asks a deceptively simple question: is a graph B found inside a parent graph A? Famously NP-complete and the subject of volumes of study, attempts to practically solve subgraph problems typically require specialized software or the focused application of problem-specific theoretical knowledge. Here we present a straightforward linear framework that neatly joins SGI to lattice theory and constrained satisfiability and, importantly, yields an easily implemented algorithm that naturally leverages consumer-grade hardware and off-the-shelf libraries to compete with state-of-the-art specialized solvers. We additionally show practical realizations in approachable settings, along with some benchmarks that reduce 6+ hour computations to seconds. Aimed at readability, we develop a series of computable algebraic invariants and demonstrate their application to familiar problems such as the Knight's Tour, with a focus on providing an accessible entry point for researchers in graph theory, abstract algebra, and students in general.

item.title: Identifying codes of Archimedean grids
item.description: An identifying code of a graph is a dominating set $C$ such that the sets $N[v]\cap C$ are pairwise distinct. The minimum density of an identifying code has been studied extensively for several infinite grids. It is known to be $1/4$ for the triangular grid and $7/20$ for the square grid, whereas for the hexagonal grid the problem is still open, between $5/12$ and $53/126$. These three grids are the regular members of the family of the eleven Archimedean grids. In this paper, we start a systematic study of identifying codes in this family. We determine the minimum density for five of the nine Archimedean grids for which it was not known: it is $2/3$ for the truncated hexagonal grid $3.12.12$, $3/7$ for the truncated square grid $4.8.8$, and $1/3$ for the trihexagonal (kagome) grid $3.6.3.6$, the elongated triangular grid $3^3.4^2$ and the snub hexagonal grid $3^4.6$. All lower bounds are proved by the discharging method. For the three remaining non-regular Archimedean grids, we also obtain some bounds: the minimum density lies between $3/7$ and $13/30$ for the truncated trihexagonal grid $4.6.12$, between $1/3$ and $11/30$ for the rhombitrihexagonal grid $3.4.6.4$, and between $2/7$ and $9/28$ for the snub square grid $3^2.4.3.4$.

item.title: Near-Optimal Bounds for Testing k-Colorability
item.description: We study the sample complexity of testing $k$-colorability in the dense graph model. A graph is $\varepsilon$-far from being $k$-colorable if at least $\varepsilon n^2$ edge deletions are required to make it $k$-colorable. We prove that, for every integer $k\ge 2$, a uniformly random induced subgraph on \[ O\!\left(\frac{k\log k}{\varepsilon}\right) \] vertices is non-$k$-colorable with probability at least $2/3$ whenever the original graph is $\varepsilon$-far from $k$-colorable. The proof introduces a trial coloring process based on nested palette systems and iteratively selected pivots. This yields an upper bound of $O(k\log k/\varepsilon)$, which is no worse than the previous state of the art $O(k\log(1/\varepsilon)/\varepsilon)$ throughout the nonvacuous parameter range, and is an improvement whenever $1/\varepsilon$ is superpolynomial in $k$. Moreover, for every fixed $k$, our bound matches the known lower bound, thereby establishing the optimal $Θ(1/\varepsilon)$ dependence on $\varepsilon$ and, to the best of our knowledge, achieving this optimal dependence for the first time.

item.title: Kempe Reachability with $k\geq 3$ Colors Is $\mathsf{PSPACE}$-Complete on Claw-Free Graphs
item.description: A \emph{proper vertex coloring} assigns colors to vertices so that adjacent vertices have distinct colors. A \emph{Kempe change} in a proper vertex coloring exchanges two colors on one component of the subgraph induced by the vertices of those colors. For a fixed palette of $k$ colors, \textsc{Kempe Reachability} asks whether two given proper vertex colorings of the same graph are connected by a sequence of Kempe changes. This problem is known to be $\mathsf{PSPACE}$-complete for every fixed $k\geq 3$. A graph is \emph{claw-free} if no vertex has three pairwise nonadjacent neighbors. The \emph{line graph} of a graph has one vertex for each edge, with two vertices adjacent exactly when the corresponding edges share an end. Line graphs are claw-free, and their Kempe changes correspond to \emph{edge-Kempe changes} in the original graph, which exchange two colors on one component of the subgraph formed by the edges of those colors. A claw-free graph with a proper $k$-coloring has maximum degree at most $2k-2$, whereas for $k\geq 4$ all proper $k$-colorings of a graph of maximum degree at most $k$ are connected by Kempe changes. We show that, for every fixed $k\geq 3$, \textsc{Kempe Reachability} with $k$ colors is $\mathsf{PSPACE}$-complete even on line graphs of connected simple $k$-regular graphs, and hence even on connected $(2k-2)$-regular claw-free graphs. Equivalently, deciding whether two proper $k$-edge-colorings are connected by edge-Kempe changes is $\mathsf{PSPACE}$-complete even on connected simple $k$-regular graphs. ChatGPT 6 Pro and Claude Fable 5.1 were used to assist with developing and reviewing mathematical arguments and drafting and revising the paper. The author takes full responsibility for the correctness and content of the paper.

item.title: A Polynomial-Time Algorithm for $k$-Path Vertex Cover Reconfiguration on Trees under Token Sliding
item.description: A $k$-path vertex cover ($k$-PVC) of a graph is a set of vertices meeting every path on $k$ vertices. In Token Sliding, one token occupies each vertex of a cover; a move slides one token along an edge to an unoccupied vertex, preserving the cover property. We study whether two covers of a tree are joined by such moves. The case $k=2$ admits a linear-time decision algorithm. For every integer $k\geq2$, we give an $O(kn^2)$-time decision algorithm on trees of order $n$, with $k$ part of the input. Two covers are reachable precisely when their rigid tokens, which never move, occupy the same set and every component remaining after their deletion has the same token count. The proof transforms configurations of equal size without rigid tokens into a canonical configuration built on properly rooted subtrees, whose paths on $k$ vertices pass through their roots. A rooted-subtree recurrence identifies movable candidate tokens. We also give a direct recursive construction between the supplied endpoints, returning at most $8n^2\,3^{\lceil n/2\rceil}$ slides in $O(n^{10}3^{n/2})$ time. ChatGPT 6 Pro and Claude Fable 5.1 were used to assist with developing and reviewing mathematical arguments and drafting and revising the paper. The author takes full responsibility for the correctness and content of the paper.

item.title: Almost tight distributed approximation for domination in sparse graph classes
item.description: We study distributed approximation of Minimum Dominating Set in a very general class of sparse graphs, extending near-optimal approximation results from the minor-free setting to bounded expansion. In more detail, for fixed $d$ and $\varepsilon>0$, we give a new deterministic constant-round LOCAL algorithm for Minimum Dominating Set on graphs of maximum average degree at most $d$ and bounded depth-one shallow-minor density. Its approximation ratio is $d+1+\varepsilon$, which is optimal up to $\varepsilon$ for every even integer $d\geq 2$. This improves on the recent results of Amiri and Siebertz by extending beyond proper minor-closed classes. From this algorithm, we derive almost-tight constant-round approximations for a number of graph classes. We get $(7+\varepsilon)$-approximations for planar graphs and graphs of bounded Euler genus, and $(5+\varepsilon)$-approximations for their triangle-free subclasses. This answers the $7+\varepsilon$ question of Wawrzyniak positively, and matches the recent results of Amiri and Siebertz. We also apply our algorithm to classes of bounded queue-number or stack-number, obtaining bounds that are tight up to $\varepsilon$. Additionally, we answer questions of Amiri and Siebertz about improving the dependence of the round complexity on $1/\varepsilon$ and obtaining polynomial local computation for fixed parameters, when comparing the output to the usual domination number.

item.title: Links of minimum degree and exact covering numbers
item.description: The covering number $C(v,k,t)$ is the least number of $k$-subsets, called blocks, of a $v$-set such that every $t$-subset lies in one of them. We reduce the question whether a covering with $L$ blocks exists to the classification of links. If every point of such a covering lies in at least $r$ blocks and $(r+1)v>kL$, some point lies in exactly $r$ blocks, and its link, the blocks through it with the point removed, is a $(v-1,k-1,t-1)$-covering with $r$ blocks. It then suffices to list these links up to isomorphism, to prove the list complete, and to show that no link in the list extends to a covering with $L$ blocks. Completeness is certified by one unsatisfiable formula that excludes the listed classes, so the program that lists the links need not be trusted. In general the last two steps are decided by propositional satisfiability (SAT) solving, with every formula written by two separately implemented encoders and every refutation checked by a formally verified proof checker. For links with four blocks and $t=3$ we give the classification by hand, under a condition on the parameters. As an application we determine twenty-five covering numbers with $t\in\{3,4,5\}$ in which the published lower bound was one less than the size of a known covering, among them $C(39,24,3)=9$.

item.title: On Multi-label radio Labelings of Graphs
item.description: We propose and study a multi-labeling generalization of the $k$-radio labeling problem of graphs: given a graph $G$ and integers $k$ and $m$, assign to each vertex of $G$ a set of $m$ integer labels such that distinct labels assigned to a vertex differ by at least $k+1$, and the labels of any two distinct vertices $x$ and $y$ pairwise differ by at least $k+1-d(x,y)$, with $d(x,y)$ being the distance between vertices $x$ and $y$. We prove general bounds on the minimum span of such a labeling and more refined results for the case $k=1$. For paths and cycles, we derive sharp bounds on the minimum span when $k$ is small. We finally propose a conjecture for the minimum span on the path and for an almost-tight bound on the cycle.

item.title: Euclidean Embeddings of Acyclic Hypergraph Line Metrics
item.description: We study Euclidean embeddings of higher-order line metrics arising from hypergraphs. For a fixed threshold \(s\geq 1\), the \(s\)-line graph \(L_s(H)\) has one vertex for each hyperedge of \(H\), with two hyperedges adjacent when they intersect in at least \(s\) vertices; its shortest-path metric is the native \(s\)-line metric. In the unrestricted setting, every finite graph occurs as the \(s\)-line graph of some hypergraph, so the worst-case Euclidean distortion is \(Θ(\log n)\). We show that \(α\)-acyclicity yields a sharp improvement to \(Θ(\sqrt{\log\log n})\). Although the canonical join tree of an \(α\)-acyclic hypergraph may have arbitrarily large stretch relative to the native metric, we prove that for every \(s\), the \(s\)-line graphs of \(α\)-acyclic hypergraphs are exactly the dually chordal graphs. Using their constant-factor spanning-tree approximations together with classical tree-embedding bounds, we obtain an \(O(\sqrt{\log\log n})\) Euclidean embedding bound. We then show this is asymptotically tight by realizing every finite tree as the \(s\)-line graph of an \(α\)-acyclic hypergraph. Thus, the worst-case distortion is \(Θ(\sqrt{\log\log n})\), including for hypergraphs of rank at most \(3s+1\).

item.title: Optimal single-track Gray codes from Gray-ordered necklaces
item.description: A single-track Gray code of length $n$ is a cyclic Gray code of $n$-bit words in which every column is a cyclic shift of the first. For prime $n$ the longest possible period is $2^n-2$. Whether it is attained for every prime has been open since Hiltgen, Paterson and Brandestini introduced these codes in 1996, and optimal codes were known for primes $n\le 19$. We show that a conjecture of Degni and Drisko (2007) on the reflected Gray code order of necklaces implies optimal single-track Gray codes for every prime. Their list of necklaces, conjecturally a Gray path for prime $n$, closes into a Hamilton cycle of the necklace graph after $(n-3)/2$ explicit Pósa rotations, and such a cycle lifts to an optimal code. This implication is formalized in Lean 4. Together with computation it gives optimal single-track Gray codes for every odd prime $n\le 47$: for $n\le 37$ explicit codes checked word by word by a program independent of the generator, and for $n=41$, $43$ and $47$ codes obtained from the implication after the Degni-Drisko property was verified at these lengths by two independently written programs.

item.title: Barrier Log-Concavity of Large Forests
item.description: We prove that the independence sequence of every sufficiently large forest is strictly barrier log-concave: whenever $i_{k+1}>i_k$, one has $i_k^2>i_{k-1}i_{k+1}$. Consequently, every common downward coefficient tilt is unimodal, with one order threshold valid simultaneously for all $0<t\le1$. As an application, we prove that every sufficiently large well-covered tree has a strictly log-concave independence polynomial. More generally, the latter conclusion holds for well-covered forests with sufficiently large matching number. Every sufficiently large forest with a palindromic independence polynomial is also strictly log-concave, with its modes at the central ranks. The proof establishes local coefficient-curvature estimates uniformly over forests of unbounded maximum degree and over activities tending to zero. Combined with the fixed-density theorem of Fang, Lu, Nevo, Yao, and Zheng, these estimates complete the strict log-concavity interval down to rank one through $\lfloor17α/25\rfloor$; the terminal fraction is inherited. The classical decreasing tail then yields the barrier property. A cumulative-coefficient corona theorem transfers barrier log-concavity of the base forest to full strict log-concavity of its leaf corona.

item.title: A Linear-Time Algorithm for the Unbiased Claw Game on Graphs with Maximum Degree 4
item.description: We study the unbiased Maker-Breaker $K_{1,3}$-game, the unbiased claw game, played on the edge set of a general graph $G$. In this game, Maker and Breaker alternatingly claim edges of $G$, and Maker wins if his claimed edges contain a claw once no more edges are available. Graphs with maximum degree at least 5 are Maker's win. A graph $G$ is claw-connected if the hypergraph modeling the unbiased claw game played on $G$ is connected. We characterize Maker's win in the unbiased claw game on every claw-connected graph whose maximum degree is different from 3. Our main structural result is a complete characterization of Maker's win for claw-connected graphs with exactly one vertex of degree 4. The analysis is based on the fact that vertices of degree 4 act as forcing structures. Our characterization results in a linear-time algorithm for the unbiased claw game on claw-connected graphs with maximum degree different from 3. We also obtain a linear-time decomposition algorithm reducing the game on general graphs to a collection of pairwise edge-disjoint claw-connected subgraphs of maximum degree exactly 3, thereby isolating the only remaining case. This decomposition yields an $\mathcal{O}(|V(G)|^3)$-time algorithm for the unbiased claw game on general graphs, improving on the $\mathcal{O}(|V(G)|^7)$-time algorithm implied by the work of Galliot, Gravier and Sivignon (arXiv 2026). For a lower bound on the decision complexity, we prove that any agent deciding the game in the adjacency-array model makes at least $Ω(|V(G)|)$ queries in the worst case, indicating the optimality of our linear-time algorithm.

item.title: Metric Dimension is NP-complete on Graphs of Treewidth Two
item.description: The metric dimension of a connected graph is the least number of vertices whose distance vectors distinguish all vertices. We show that deciding whether the metric dimension of a graph is at most a given integer is NP-complete on graphs of treewidth at most two. As the problem is polynomial on trees, the graphs of treewidth one, this settles the treewidth threshold of its hardness, which was known to lie between two and twenty-four. The reduction is from satisfiability of formulas in which every literal occurs at most twice. To such a formula with $n$ clauses and $r$ variables it associates a graph $G_\varphi$ of treewidth at most two with $O((n+r)^2)$ vertices, whose metric dimension is $2(n+r)+5$ if the formula is satisfiable and $2(n+r)+6$ otherwise.

item.title: Claw-Free and Line Graph Edge Deletion on Block Graphs
item.description: Edge deletion problems ask for the fewest edges whose deletion gives a graph with a specified property. We study two such problems on block graphs. First making the graph claw-free, and second making it a line graph. Since every line graph is claw-free, the second problem is at least as difficult as the first. We show that on block graphs the two optimum values are always equal, and both are attained by the line graph of a forest. The main step is a completion argument, in which starting from any claw-free solution, we put back edges to get some nice structure inside each block still maintaining the claw-free property. This reduces both edge-deletion problems to the same problem of selecting vertices within the blocks of the input graph. We solve it by dynamic programming in $O(n+m)$ time, which also produces an optimal deletion set and a forest whose line graph is what remains after the completion argument. We also extend the method to $K_{1,r+1}$-free edge deletion for every fixed $r$.

item.title: Nonlinear fixed-distance codes via real lifts of moment configurations
item.description: Let $A_q(n,d)$ denote the largest size of a code of length $n$ and minimum Hamming distance $d$ over an alphabet of $q$ symbols. For fixed $q\ge2$ and $d\ge4$ we construct codes with redundancy $n-\log_q A_q(n,d)\le(d-3)\log_q n+O(\sqrt{\log n})$ for all large $n$. No algebraic structure is imposed on the alphabet, and the codes are not linear. For $d=4$ and $d=5$ the coefficient of $\log_q n$ matches the Hamming bound, so the redundancy is determined up to lower-order terms. At distance four the codes are provably better than every linear code: by the polynomial-method bound for cap sets, $\mathbb{F}_q$-linear codes with $q>2$ require a strictly larger coefficient in front of $\log_q n$. The construction imposes moment checksums over an auxiliary finite field, as BCH codes do, but one fewer than the distance would normally require. The affine-line theorem from prior work describes the dependencies left by these checks. We exclude them by placing the code positions inside a specially structured subset of the field, built from Behrend's sphere construction with the help of algebraic number theory.

item.title: The Two-Level Poset Game is PSPACE-Complete
item.description: Poset games form a fundamental class of combinatorial games that includes classical games such as Nim and Chomp. Determining the outcome of a poset game is known to be PSPACE-complete even for posets of height at most three. However, the exact computational complexity of Two-Level Poset Game, played on posets of height at most two, has remained an open problem for over a decade. We resolve this problem by proving that Two-Level Poset Game is PSPACE-complete via a polynomial-time reduction from Avoid True on positive CNF formulas.

item.title: A Randomized Approximation Algorithm for Doubly Free-Boundary Macdonald Processes
item.description: We construct an approximate sampler for finite doubly free-boundary Macdonald rail-yard processes with Macdonald, boundary, and edge parameters in $(0,1)$. The construction allows arbitrary finite sequences of additions and removals of horizontal or vertical strips and all four boundary types. It reverses a finite commutation--reflection history from a partition sequence whose entries are equal, with the common partition weighted by both boundaries. We derive local reconstruction kernels from the skew Cauchy, Littlewood, and branching identities. Bulk and boundary updates combine integer increments with conditional shape sampling at a prescribed size; same-sign swaps use finite conditional resampling. For $K$ reflection periods and an initial partition-size cutoff $M$, the algorithm terminates almost surely and samples the resulting approximating law exactly. We prove total variation convergence to the target process as $K,M\to\infty$ and give explicit bounds for both truncation errors, decaying geometrically in the cutoffs for fixed input parameters. Under fixed parameter bounds, we also bound the expected operation count of direct enumeration in a unit-cost model. We further construct an exact rejection sampler for the initial partition law without a size cutoff or evaluation of its normalizing constant. Using this sampler removes the size-truncation error, leaving only the error from the finite reflection history.

item.title: Dynamic Run-Out Pricing for Perishable Goods
item.description: I study a dynamic pricing problem in which a seller with limited inventory must sequentially price a perishable product for arriving customers with heterogeneous valuations. The key difficulty lies in balancing immediate sales against future opportunities under capacity constraints and stochastic customer valuations. I propose a simple, interpretable, and asymptotically optimal dynamic pricing algorithm, called Dynamic Run-Out Pricing (DROP), that adjusts prices in real time based on current inventory and anticipated future demand. Under the assumption that customers' valuations follow bounded or exponential distributions, our theoretical results show that DROP's expected revenue converges to the optimal revenue as market size grows. Unlike traditional notions of near-optimality, where the ratio of the algorithm's revenue to the optimal revenue converges to 1, I show that the absolute difference between the two revenues converges to 0 as the market size increases, underscoring the algorithm's effectiveness. Furthermore, I extend our analysis to heavy-tailed valuation distributions, specifically the Pareto distribution, where standard run-out heuristics severely underprice inventory by ignoring the value of waiting for extreme valuations. To correct this, I introduce the Tail-Aware DROP (TA-DROP) heuristic, which intentionally inflates prices to protect inventory, and I prove that it restores asymptotic optimality with a strict polynomial convergence rate.

item.title: A note on Finiteness and Boundedness in Cartesian Products of Discrete and Well-Ordered Sets, Application to Transition Systems
item.description: In this short note, we prove that any closed interval in a well-ordered and discrete space is finite. The coincidence between finiteness and boundedness can then be established for transition systems where the state space is well-ordered and discrete. Finally, this result is also proven when the state space is a Cartesian product of $d$ discrete and well-ordered sets.

item.title: A Four-by-Four Obstruction to Polynomial Removal for Ordered Binary Matrices
item.description: We exhibit a fixed $4\times 4$ binary matrix with no polynomial induced ordered removal bound. At depth $h\geq 1$, let $m=2^h$. Our explicit host has order $(14h+2)m$, exactly $2m^6+\frac{1}{2}(m-2)m^5$ induced copies, and exact editing distance $m^2$ cells. Its normalized editing distance is $Θ(h^{-2})$, while its induced-copy density is $Θ(4^{-h}h^{-8})$. The lower bound holds against arbitrary cell edits through an injective family of $m^2$ protected selections. An exhaustive arithmetic classification identifies every induced copy and proves that a matching canonical repair creates none. The original-copy transversal number is exactly $m$, yielding an unbounded gap between hitting existing copies and eliminating all copies. The identities and the obstruction at every depth are formalized in Lean, with verification sources included as ancillary files.

item.title: Nim heaps in the Game of Cycles: the parity conjecture fails on trees
item.description: The Game of Cycles, invented by Francis Su, is a two-player game in which the players take turns drawing arrows on the edges of a plane graph, never creating a sink or a source. On a tree only the sink-source rule matters, and the player who makes the last move wins. Several authors conjectured that on a tree the second player wins exactly when the number of markable edges is even. We show that this parity conjecture is false, and we explain why. The explanation is a hidden game of Nim: a path segment that is blocked by an arrow at one end and free at the other behaves exactly like a nim heap whose size is its length. Combined with a calculus for cutting and gluing trees at vertices next to leaves, this shows that the conjecture fails as soon as a single tree has Grundy value at least 2. The smallest counterexamples have 15 vertices. Trees with Grundy values 2 and 4 first appear at 17 vertices, and every value up to 63 occurs, which answers a question of Fokkink and Zandee. We also refute a related conjecture of Zandee. We then look closely at spiders. The spiders S(2,3,z) violate the conjecture for every z >= 14. The Grundy values of S(1,2j,z) are given by an exact formula governed by binary carries. For 99 pairs (x,y), the value of S(x,y,z) is eventually the parity of z. On the positive side, the conjecture holds for all trees in which every thread has at most two edges, and this bound is sharp. Along the way we prove a twin-branch reduction, give an algorithm that is polynomial for spiders with a fixed number of legs, and collect the questions that we could not answer. The boldest asks whether every non-negative integer is the Grundy value of some tree.

item.title: Almost every Boolean function has central threshold degree
item.description: The polynomial threshold degree (or threshold degree) of a Boolean function is the least degree of a real polynomial whose sign represents it. We prove that almost every Boolean function has polynomial threshold degree among the central one or two integers. More precisely, a uniformly chosen Boolean function on $n$ variables has threshold degree $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ or $\lceil n/2\rceil$ except with probability at most $\exp(-c2^{n/2}/n)$, for an absolute constant $c>0$ and all sufficiently large $n$. A parity example gives a lower bound on the exceptional probability whose exponent differs from ours by a factor of order $n$. The proof relates polynomial sign representation to recovery of Reed--Muller codes from random erasures, and combines sharp-threshold estimates with bounds on generalized Hamming weights and minimum distance.

item.title: Coefficientwise Extremality and Rigidity for Independent Sets in Bipartite Graph Covers
item.description: Let $G$ be a finite bipartite graph and let $\widetilde G$ be an $M$-fold cover. We compare independent sets of $\widetilde G$ with those of the trivial cover, consisting of $M$ disjoint copies of $G$, after prescribing how many vertices are selected above each vertex of $G$. A conjecture from 2011, motivated by the Bethe approximation, asserts that the trivial cover maximizes every such count. We prove this for every feasible occupation profile whose active graph has treewidth at most two or is chordal bipartite. Equality holds exactly when the restricted cover is flat, meaning that fibre relabelings make it trivial. For $M\ge2$ and positive feasible occupations, a nonflat cover of a connected bipartite graph of treewidth at most two has a deficit of at least twice the coefficient of $p_G^{M-2}$ with every occupation reduced by one. A holonomy-dependent bound improves the factor to three for odd-order holonomy; both uniform constants are sharp. Comparison and rigidity survive finite compositions along an edge or a vertex, and quantitative bounds from one piece propagate to the whole graph, giving results beyond the two original classes. On any bipartite base, the first nonzero homogeneous defect is determined by the shortest cycles with nontrivial holonomy. At singleton occupations, our counts are numbers of DP-colorings of full covers. The dual DP color function on these classes and their finite seam compositions equals the chromatic polynomial, with equality attained precisely by canonical labelings. Dong's chromatic-polynomial inequality then yields the Dual-DP Shameful inequality on the same graph class. The main theorems have been formalized in Lean 4.

item.title: Maximally symmetric $(23_4)$ configurations and the end of the existence problem for geometric $(n_4)$ configurations
item.description: A geometric $(n_4)$ configuration is a set of $n$ points and $n$ lines in the real projective plane such that every point lies on exactly four of the lines and every line contains exactly four of the points. The question of which $n$ admit such a configuration was posed by Grünbaum in 2000, following his 1990 paper with Rigby that gave the first geometric $4$-configuration, a $(21_4)$. Successive work of Bokowski-Schewe, of Bokowski, Grünbaum and Schewe, of Bokowski-Pilaud, and of Cuntz settled every case but one. Cuntz's 2018 paper, which constructed $(22_4)$ and $(26_4)$ configurations, states that only $n=23$ remained open. We settle this last case. We prove that for every prime $n\equiv3\pmod4$, in particular for $n=23$, the group of projective symmetries of a geometric $(n_4)$ configuration has order at most four, which explains why $n=23$ resisted the symmetric constructions that settled the other values. Reducing the case of a Klein four-group of symmetries to a few thousand bilinear polynomial systems in $18$ unknowns, and solving all of them exactly with Gröbner bases and saturation, we show that exactly two geometric $(23_4)$ configurations reach this bound, up to projective equivalence, and that there are no others even over $\mathbb{C}$. Both are self-polar with respect to a conic. The first has integer homogeneous coordinates; the second is defined over $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{17})$, but not over $\mathbb{Q}$. Consequently geometric $(n_4)$ configurations exist if and only if $n\ge18$ and $n\ne19$. A third configuration, self-polar and defined over a real cubic field, has only a single symmetry of order two. The same classification at $n=22$ and $n=26$ recovers Cuntz's configurations and finds three new combinatorial types at $n=22$ and $94$ at $n=26$, among them a $(26_4)$ configuration that is self-polar with respect to a conic without real points.

item.title: Lower bounds for Ramsey numbers: $\mathrm{R}(6,8)\ge 135$ and $\mathrm{R}(8,10)\ge 345$
item.description: We prove the lower bounds $\mathrm{R}(6,8)\ge 135$ and $\mathrm{R}(8,10)\ge 345$, improving the bounds 134 and 343 listed in the April 2026 revision of Radziszowski's dynamic survey. We give explicit red/blue colorings of $K_{134}$ with no red $K_6$ or blue $K_8$, and of $K_{344}$ with no red $K_8$ or blue $K_{10}$, and verify them with two independently written exhaustive clique checkers. Starting from published colorings, we find these witnesses by adding vertices and repairing the resulting monochromatic cliques through local search. The search uses exact conflict counts, preparation moves aimed at making remaining cliques cheaper to break, and mutations followed by repair. A loss based on the largest monochromatic clique containing each edge yielded a useful intermediate state for the $\mathrm{R}(6,8)$ construction. Guided by the author, an AI coding agent wrote and ran the search code; we describe the methods and document the ancestry of the resulting colorings.

item.title: Integer programming on polytopes of Chvátal rank one is as hard as lattice problems
item.description: A rational polyhedron has Chvátal rank at most one if a single round of Chvátal-Gomory cuts yields its integer hull. For such polyhedra, integer feasibility is in NP $\cap$ coNP by a result of Boyd and Pulleyblank from the early 1980s, so it is unlikely to be NP-hard. Whether it is polynomial has remained open since then. We answer this question negatively, under either of two standard assumptions from lattice-based cryptography. First, a polynomial-time algorithm for this problem would solve bounded distance decoding with polynomial factors in deterministic polynomial time, contradicting a widely believed conjecture. Second, assuming the hardness of learning with errors, an average-case analogue of bounded distance decoding, the problem is also hard on average, for an efficiently samplable distribution of polytopes. Both results rest on an elementary sufficient condition: a polyhedron has Chvátal rank at most one if its width is less than one along every row of some unimodular matrix. For our polytopes, such a matrix exists but is hard to find.

item.title: Tweaking the constant in the Linear Hadwiger Theorem
item.description: Norin and Steiner recently proved the Linear Hadwiger Conjecture. That is, there is an absolute constant $C$ such that every graph $G$ satisfies $χ(G)\leqslant C\,\text{had}(G)$, where $χ(G)$ is the chromatic number and $\text{had}(G)$ is the Hadwiger number of $G$. Their proof gives a non-optimised constant $C$ of order $10^{100}$. This paper uses extensive AI-based optimisation to show that every graph $G$ satisfies $χ(G) \leqslant 19{,}885{,}160\,\text{had}(G)$.

item.title: Decomposition Profiles and Weisfeiler-Leman Dimension for Graphs of Bounded Rank Width
item.description: The Weisfeiler-Leman (WL) algorithm tests graph isomorphism by assigning colours to $d$-tuples of vertices and iteratively refining the colouring according to neighbourhood configurations until it stabilizes. Increasing $d$ allows the test to detect finer structural differences between graphs, but the computational cost grows exponentially with $d$. The central question is which dimension allows us to distinguish nonisomorphic graphs. We relate a sufficient such dimension to the structure of a graph $G$ through a rank decomposition over $\mathbb F_2$. The two parameters governing the bound are the maximum cut rank $w$ and the fork load $\ell$, which is the largest sum of the parent and two child cut ranks at a fork in the decomposition tree. We prove that WL in dimension $\max\{\ell+1,2w+2\}$ distinguishes every finite nonempty vertex-coloured graph $G$ with such a decomposition from every graph not isomorphic to $G$. Consequently, for $k\geq1$, graphs of rank width at most $k$ can be distinguished from every nonisomorphic graph in dimension $3k+1$, graphs of linear rank width at most $k$ in dimension $2k+2$, and edgeless graphs in dimension one. Uncoloured Cai-Fürer-Immerman (CFI) constructions give linear lower bounds for both width parameters, so the upper bounds are tight up to constant factors.

item.title: Mixing Times of Switch Chains via High-Dimensional Expansion
item.description: The switch chain is a Markov chain defined on the set of labelled realizations of a given graphical degree sequence. At each step, a pair of vertex-disjoint edges is chosen at random and the process attempts to replace them with a uniformly chosen perfect matching of the same four vertices, rejecting any proposal that would create a multiple edge. The resulting process is reversible with respect to the uniform distribution on all realizations. We investigate the mixing time of this chain by viewing realizations as the facets of a simplicial complex and studying a variant of the original process called the simplicial switch chain, which we analyze using tools from the theory of high-dimensional expansion. Our technical contributions include a proof that links of faces of sufficiently high codimension are strong spectral expanders and a comparison between the Dirichlet energies of large block updates and two-edge updates. Our main result is an $O(Δ^{2}m\log m)$ bound on the mixing time of both simplicial and classical switch chains whenever $m\ge CΔ^{8}$, where $m$ is the number of edges, $Δ$ is the maximum prescribed degree, and $C>0$ is an absolute constant. For sequences on $n$ vertices with fixed maximum degree, this proves that the chain mixes in $O(n\log n)$ steps, resolving a longstanding conjecture of Cooper, Dyer, and Greenhill and extending its conclusion to irregular degree sequences.

item.title: An Efficient Algorithm for the Quickest Path Reliability Problem
item.description: The quickest path reliability problem is to compute the probability that a given flow is transmitted along a single source-destination path within a given time limit. When a budget is imposed, path feasibility is jointly dependent on lead time, transmission cost, and capacity. Existing exact methods may require enumeration of all minimal paths a priori or examination of many partial paths that cannot be completed feasibly. In this paper, we propose an exact algorithm that generates the corresponding lower boundary state vectors without first enumerating minimal paths. Shortest-lead-time, least-cost, and widest-capacity information yield admissible destination-based bounds. Stronger capacity-aware bounds are derived from capacity-filtered subnetworks. These bounds allow early pruning of infeasible branches while keeping all solutions. The algorithm generates the exact complete set of lower bounds without any duplicates, and its correctness and computational complexity are proven.

item.title: An upper bound of 4.268 for the random 3-SAT satisfiability threshold
item.description: We prove that a random 3-SAT formula with $n$ variables and $\lfloor 4.268n\rfloor$ clauses is unsatisfiable with high probability. The satisfiability threshold has attracted considerable attention: successive upper bounds reached 4.4898 in the work of Díaz, Kirousis, Mitsche, and Pérez-Giménez, while the cavity method predicts a value near 4.267. Our bound brings the rigorous upper estimate close to this prediction. The proof builds on earlier interpolation methods, including the energetic approach of Achlioptas and Menchaca-Méndez. We study the smallest number of clauses that any assignment must violate, comparing the random formula with a simpler system of constraints on individual variables. This comparison reduces the bound to a finite calculation, which we verify using exact rational arithmetic. The proof is formalized in Lean 4.

item.title: Dijkstra Is NOT Greedy: A Global-to-Local Proof of Correctness
item.description: Dijkstra's algorithm is almost universally classified as a canonical greedy algorithm. This paper challenges that conventional interpretation and presents a simple, direct proof of correctness from a different viewpoint. Contrary to the widespread intuition that the algorithm repeatedly makes a local choice and thereby reaches a global optimum, we show that the logical direction can be read in exactly the opposite way: at each iteration, the algorithm identifies a globally shortest path among all paths whose destinations remain unsolved, and the endpoint of that globally shortest path is therefore solved as a ``local'' shortest-path problem. In other words, the local shortest path is obtained as an immediate consequence of a global minimum. Based on this observation, we formulate a Three-Step Exclusion Method that interprets Dijkstra's iteration as deterministic contraction of the global path space. The resulting proof highlights optimal substructure, boundary-state reduction, and dynamic-programming structure, and offers a conceptually simple alternative to the usual greedy explanation.

item.title: Distinguishing graphs with simple spectrum by homomorphism counts
item.description: We study which graph classes determine every graph with simple spectrum up to isomorphism by homomorphism counts from their members. We show that such a class has unbounded treewidth and Euler genus and contains a graph with the complete graph on seven vertices as a minor. To prove these conditions, we construct pairs of non-isomorphic cospectral graphs with simple spectrum, each bipartite, nonsingular and of maximum degree at most six. The construction attaches rooted trees to Cai-Furer-Immerman graphs and preserves homomorphism indistinguishability over every minor-closed class. We then prove that subcubic homomorphism counts determine every graph whose adjacency matrix has kernel dimension at most one. This extends the known result for nonsingular graphs and applies to all graphs with simple spectrum. We also prove that two graphs have the same subcubic homomorphism counts if and only if they have the same number of vertices and there is a bijective linear isometry between the images of their adjacency matrices that intertwines the adjacency operators and preserves the coordinatewise trilinear forms. Finally, we prove that homomorphism counts from the single-vertex graph and from subdivisions of any sequence of connected cubic graphs have the same distinguishing power as subcubic homomorphism counts if every complete graph is a minor of some member of the sequence.

item.title: A symmetric conference matrix of order 86
item.description: We construct a symmetric conference matrix of order $86$, the smallest order for which existence was open. Equivalently, there exist a conference graph with parameters $(85,42,20,21)$, a regular two-graph on $86$ points, and a real equiangular tight frame of $86$ vectors in $\mathbb{R}^{43}$. The matrix is a $12\times12$ array of $7\times7$ circulants with two border rows, and it admits a group of automorphisms of order $21$. Its $86$ descendants give exactly ten nonisomorphic strongly regular graphs.

item.title: A note on the list chromatic number of two matroids
item.description: We study list coloring of common independent sets of two matroids. We construct a graphic matroid $M_1$ and a partition matroid $M_2$ with common chromatic number two and common list chromatic number three, showing that the two parameters need not be equal. This resolves a question raised by Király, later stated as a conjecture by Aharoni, Berger, Guo, and Kotlar. We also show that if two strongly base-orderable matroids are each $2$-colorable, then their intersection is $2$-list-colorable.

item.title: Recognizers for Graph-Encoding Languages
item.description: We introduce recurrent incidence automata (RIAs), a new automaton model motivated by a decomposition of certain two-stack visibly pushdown computations. The decomposition separates vertex-local finite-state computations from recurrent one-stack interfaces connecting consecutive vertices. The construction is motivated by a two-stack visibly pushdown encoding of arbitrary ordered graphs whose strings admit a unique factorization into center-foldable vertex-local factors and whose auxiliary stack is empty at every factor boundary. Folding each factor into a sequence of pair symbols yields a local interface transformation. An RIA consists of a finite-state unit that computes these transformations and a recurrent layer that composes them across consecutive factors. Rather than manipulating an internal pushdown store, RIAs externalize long-range stack memory into recurrent interfaces between local computations. We show that nondeterministic RIA languages are closed under union, intersection, concatenation, Kleene-*, and reversal. Deterministic RIAs are closed under Boolean operations, although emptiness remains undecidable.

item.title: Hiding a Vertex from the Temporal Explorer: A Lower Bound for Degree-Bounded Temporal Graphs
item.description: A temporal graph is a sequence of graphs on a common set of $n$ vertices, its snapshots, one for each time step. An agent, knowing the entire sequence in advance, may at each time step wait or move along an edge of the current snapshot, and the temporal graph is explored once the agent has visited every vertex. We consider always-connected temporal graphs, in which every snapshot is connected, and ask how long exploration can be forced to take when the underlying graph, the union of all snapshots, has maximum degree at most~$Δ$. Two lower bounds were known in this setting, $Ω(Δn)$ and $Ω(n\log n)$, realised by different constructions. We establish a stronger lower bound, answering a question of Bastide, Groenland, Michel and Rambaud. Specifically, for every $n$ and $Δ$ with $Δ_0\leΔ\le n-1$ we construct an always-connected temporal graph on $n$ vertices with underlying maximum degree at most~$Δ$ that cannot be explored in fewer than $γ\,Δn\,(1+\log(n/Δ))$ time steps from any start vertex, where $γ>0$ and $Δ_0$ are absolute constants. The construction is deterministic, and every snapshot is a spanning tree with exactly one vertex of degree greater than three. Time is divided into phases. In each phase, a rotating-cycle gadget prevents the agent from reaching more than half of the trees attached to it. Between phases, we reassign target vertices among these trees using walks on a constant-degree expander, and a Gray code order of the targets keeps the underlying degree bounded. The reassignment guarantees that, for any walk of the agent, some target remains unvisited throughout all phases.

item.title: Less is Moore
item.description: A Moore graph simultaneously asks for two things that normally pull in opposite directions: every vertex should have many neighbors, while every pair of vertices should remain close. For diameter two and degree $k$, the Moore bound is $k^2+1$, and equality forces a remarkably rigid graph: it is strongly regular with parameters $(k^2+1,k,0,1)$. Hoffman and Singleton showed that such a graph can exist only for $k=2,3,7$, and possibly 57. The degree-57 case on 3,250 vertices remains open. This paper is not an attempt to settle that open problem. Instead, we ask a more algorithmic question: How efficiently can the defining Moore structure itself be searched exactly? We begin from a human-developed exhaustive search based on the radius-two Moore tree. Leaves fall into $k$ groups of size $k-1$, and the edges between every pair of such groups form a perfect matching - a permutation. For efficiency, a partial construction is abandoned immediately when it creates a triangle or quadrangle. We then describe a sequence of exact algorithm-engineering improvements developed through a human-guided AI process and accepted only after mathematical checking and controlled regression tests. The main steps are reversible short-cycle forbid counters, bit-parallel domains, minimum-remaining-value branching, singleton propagation, matching-based AllDifferent filtering, balanced replayable parallel frontiers, residual-symmetry orbit pruning, and canonical deduplication of frontier states. On the principal $k=9$ benchmark, stronger symmetry cuts wall time from 47.6 to 17.9 seconds on a six-core laptop setup. Further parallelization speedup is reported separately; on a 16-core/32-thread machine, median wall time is reduced to 5.28 seconds. Degrees 10 and 57 are used as stress tests, and a five-minute degree-57 run uses only 161 MiB peak resident memory, showing that state size is modest.

item.title: Removing $m$ from $m$-pile Divisor Nim
item.description: In Divisor Nim, a player removes from one heap a positive number of stones that divides the size of every other heap. We prove that the Sprague--Grundy (SG) value satisfies $g(P)\le 2h_{\min}+\lfloor\log_2h_{\min}\rfloor$, where $h_{\min}$ is the smallest nonempty heap, independently of the number and sizes of the other heaps. The proof starts with odd heaps and classifies removals by their factors of $2$. The largest heap in a starting board then supplies an SG bound valid throughout every successor chain. When one heap varies, we sharpen Morisawa's eventual-period bound: the smallest fixed heap controls the SG value range, the number of consecutive values compared, and an increase in the varying heap that repeats legal moves. The remaining dependence on the fixed board lies in the SG periods of direct successors. Using the largest fixed heap, we derive an explicit common period for all these recursive layers. Its possible prime divisors belong to a fixed finite set, independent of heap count; their exponents remain controlled by the total fixed stones. Finally, joining boards under one shared divisor rule preserves and can tighten the SG ceiling. Minimum 2-adic depth and its count parity determine every joined outcome, and a join with at least two odd heaps has exact SG value $0$ or $1$. We close with two conjectures: $g(P)\le2h_{\min}$, and that the least eventual SG period, when one heap varies, divides $2\operatorname{lcm}(1,\ldots,h_{\max})$. Here $h_{\max}$ is the largest fixed heap, excluding the varying heap. The second claim would remove heap-count dependence from the period bound as well.

item.title: Counterexamples to the Strong Roberson Conjecture
item.description: We refute the Strong Roberson Conjecture, which asserts that adding any graph outside a class closed under minors and disjoint unions strictly increases the distinguishing power of homomorphism counts from that class. More precisely, we construct connected graphs $H$ for which counts from graphs excluding $H$ as a minor determine the number of homomorphisms from $H$ to any target graph. We also refute the analogous conjecture with immersions in place of minors. We give explicit infinite families of excluded graphs, including cubic bipartite graphs that yield counterexamples for both relations. The proof introduces a method for deriving exact homomorphism count dependence from modular equivalences. We obtain these equivalences for infinitely many primes using prime-order automorphisms of graphs that exclude their orbit quotients as minors or immersions.

item.title: Typical growth of the Füredi-Hajnal and Stanley-Wilf limits
item.description: We prove that the Füredi-Hajnal limit and the Stanley-Wilf limit of a uniformly random permutation matrix of order $k$ are at most $\exp\bigl(O(\sqrt{k}(\log k)^{5/2})\bigr)$ with probability tending to one as $k\to\infty$. This improves the bound $\exp\bigl(O(k^{2/3}(\log k)^{7/3}/(\log\log k)^{1/3})\bigr)$ of Cibulka and Kynčl. Together with the lower bound due to Fox, these bounds show that the logarithms of both limits are $k^{1/2+o(1)}$ for almost all permutations.

item.title: Computing distances in braid-move graphs, higher Bruhat orders, and oriented-matroid mutation graphs is NP-hard
item.description: A reduced word of the longest permutation $w_0\in S_m$, taken up to commutations, encodes a wiring diagram of $m$ pseudolines, and a braid move $σ_iσ_{i+1}σ_i\leftrightarrowσ_{i+1}σ_iσ_{i+1}$ flips one of its triangles. We prove that deciding whether two wiring diagrams are within a given braid-move distance is NP-complete. Equivalently, deciding flip distance is NP-complete in the higher Bruhat order $B(m,2)$, for triangle flips of marked arrangements of pseudolines, and for rhombic tilings of a $2m$-gon; this answers an open question on flip graphs of pseudoline arrangements (SODA 2024). The reduction is from Vertex Cover: for every graph $G$ we construct two wiring diagrams at braid-move distance $|D|+2\,\mathrm{VC}(G)$, where $\mathrm{VC}(G)$ is the vertex cover number of $G$ and the Hamming distance $|D|$ is the number of triples of wires whose triangles are oriented differently. The construction glues copies of a seven-wire gadget whose braid-move distance exceeds its Hamming distance by $2$; flipping either of two disjoint triangles in both diagrams removes the excess. Adding a line at infinity transfers the construction to rank-$3$ uniform oriented matroids, where two oriented matroids are adjacent in the mutation graph if their chirotopes differ in one basis; so deciding mutation distance is NP-complete in rank $3$. An iterate of Rambau's expansion of signotopes amplifies the excess and gives NP-hardness in every fixed rank $r\ge 4$. By duality we obtain the corresponding results for every fixed corank at least $3$. The same instances show that flip distance in the higher Bruhat orders $B(n,k)$ is NP-complete for every fixed $k\ge 2$.

item.title: Complexity, Bounds, and Exact Algorithms for Rainbow $k$-Domination in Regular Graphs
item.description: A rainbow $k$-dominating function assigns the empty set or exactly one of the colors $\{1\},\{2\},\ldots,\{k\}$ to each vertex of a simple graph in such a way that every vertex receiving $\emptyset$ sees all $k$ colors in its neighborhood. This model has several facility-location interpretations where colored vertices represent sites hosting different types of services, and uncolored vertices represent the beneficiaries of those services who must have access to all of them. In this paper we study this domination variant in regular graphs. First, we develop lower and upper bounds for this class of graphs, and explore their structural consequences. Then, we use those results to prove NP-completeness of a decision formulation of this problem. Additionally, we derive exact formulas for the rainbow $k$-domination number of cycles, Möbius ladders and prisms. Lastly, we develop a dynamic-programming algorithm for generalized Petersen graphs of the form $P(6t, t)$ and state two conjectures based on the output of its implementation and related integer linear programming computations.

item.title: A proof of Lehmer's permutation conjecture for neighbor-swap graphs
item.description: In 1965, D. H. Lehmer conjectured that the permutations of every multiset admit an imperfect Hamiltonian traversal by adjacent swaps: a walk in the neighbor-swap graph that visits every word, with some words visited twice in order to reach a neighbor and return. The question is posed as an unsolved research problem in Knuth's Art of Computer Programming. Verhoeff (2017) chose the stutter words, in which every domino is a double, as the words to be reached this way, and reformulated the conjecture as the Hamiltonicity of the graph $N(S)$ on the non-stutter words, with two exceptional families --- binary signatures with an odd multiplicity, and the permutations of $(2k,1,1)$ --- that admit a Hamiltonian path but no cycle. This article proves the reformulated conjecture, and with it Lehmer's conjecture. The key structure is a partition of the words into hypercubes: the swaps inside dominoes turn each class of words with the same domino contents into a hypercube, and the stutters are exactly the $0$-dimensional classes. When every multiplicity is even, Hamiltonian cycles of the hypercubes are glued along a spanning tree, with no finite check. The case of exactly one odd multiplicity reduces to the all-even case and to a theorem of Stachowiak (1992), the one inherited Hamiltonicity input, which also settles two or more odd multiplicities. The only finite ingredients are two explicit cycles, of 28 and 84 words. Every construction is implemented in Python and checked against brute-force graphs, and the proof is formalized in Lean 4 over Mathlib.

item.title: Coloring 3-colorable graphs with $O(n^{4/23})$ colors via a Gaussian-cover recursion
item.description: We give a randomized polynomial-time algorithm that colors any promised $3$-colorable graph on $n$ vertices with $\smash{O(n^{4/23}) = O(n^{0.17391\ldots})}$ colors, improving on the recent bounds of $O(n^{0.19539})$ by Bansal, Huang, and Lee and Narang and Tang who obtained $O(n^{(13-\sqrt{97})/18+ε})=O(n^{0.17506\dots + ε})$ colors for every fixed $\smash{ε>0}$. To prove our result, we start from a fixed-level semidefinite relaxation, where we use a finite-depth recursion on Gaussian covers. Fixing a root vertex, we group vertices by correlation with the root vector. Here, each step extends a cover of directions by one edge and transfers it to a successor group. Our key analytic ingredient is a variance bound for Gaussian maxima: for a maximum of $m\geq 2$ centered linear forms with coefficient norms at most $r$, mean $μ$, and variance $v$, we prove $v\leq r^2-μ^2/(2\log m)$ using Chen's Gaussian convexity theorem. Together with a variance-scale lower-tail estimate, this controls the threshold loss at each extension, which shows that root-conditioned vector colorings can either extract a large independent set from a group or bound its size, forcing a contradiction after constantly many steps. The resulting sparse-case guarantee combines with the dense progress bound of Kawarabayashi, Thorup, and Yoneda, and the recursion's numerical inequalities are verified via rational interval arithmetic.

item.title: Reversing the Mostar line-graph inequality with long pendant paths
item.description: Let $K_t$ be obtained by attaching a pendant path of length $t$ to a fixed rooted graph $K$. We prove that $\mathrm{Mo}(L(K_t))-\mathrm{Mo}(K_t)$, the difference between its line-graph and original Mostar indices, is exactly affine on each parity class beyond a sharp uniform cutoff. The slope depends on distance-level neighbor counts and is positive for every non-bipartite core. Triangle chains give infinitely many graphs with $\mathrm{Mo}(L(G))>\mathrm{Mo}(G)$ at every positive cyclomatic number $c$, with maximum degree three, resolving Alex-Indulal Problem 3.3. At zero slope, a cactus branch-mass formula decides equality; identical vertex profiles need not give identical intercepts. Fixed cores giving equality for all sufficiently long attachments exist exactly when $c$ is odd. Maximum degree three suffices, and at every even $c$ a binary-tree construction gives equality on one eventual parity class.

item.title: A Spectral Theory of Distortion in LLM Graph Reconstruction: Sharp Bounds and Empirical Characterization
item.description: Evaluations of graph reconstruction by language models typically report a single aggregate distance between the original and the reconstructed graph. We prove that for the Wasserstein distance between Laplacian spectra such a summary is bracketed by two edge counts, the net change in edge number from below and the symmetric difference from above, each scaled by $2/n$ where $n$ is the number of vertices. The bracket is sharp: its two ends coincide exactly when the reconstruction only adds edges or only deletes them, and on that class the distance is a rescaled edge count that says nothing about which edges changed. When the ends differ, the residual between the distance and the lower end is positive only if the reconstruction both invented and lost edges, which turns it into a certificate of mixed editing computable from the reported summaries alone. We characterize these regimes in 135 reconstructions produced by three open-weight models over 45 synthetic graphs. Seventy-seven outputs are one-sided and 29 mixed outputs have $X > 0$, including cases where edge count is exactly preserved while nineteen edges were simultaneously invented and lost. The three models differ in editing policy, ranging from copying the input to attempting completion at the cost of large hallucination volume, a distinction that aggregate distortion does not reveal.

item.title: Objective Transfer in Single-Node Network Criticality: Optimal Constants and Exact Separation Thresholds
item.description: When a vertex is selected as the most damaging single attack target under one damage objective, how much of the optimal damage under a different objective does it retain? We study this for the three objectives commonly used in critical node detection -- pairwise connectivity (PC), size of the largest surviving component (LCC) and number of components (NC) -- for single-vertex attacks on connected graphs, with the attacked vertex counted in the damage and ties resolved optimistically. For the pair PC, LCC the loss is bounded: a PC-optimal vertex retains at least a $2-\sqrt2$ fraction of the optimal LCC damage, an LCC-optimal vertex at least 2/3 of the optimal PC damage, and both constants are best possible. Neither bound depends on the choice among tied optimal vertices or on whether the attacked vertex is counted, and both remain valid as lower bounds for attack sets of any fixed size. For the four directions involving NC no positive constant exists; explicit families have ratios decaying like 1/k, and no single attack set retains a positive fraction of all three optima uniformly. We also determine the smallest orders at which the sets of optimal vertices become disjoint: 7 for LCC/NC, 8 for PC/NC, 9 for PC/LCC and 11 for all three pairwise, with trees realising the triple separation for every n>=11; these values rest on an exhaustive enumeration of the 11,989,762 connected graphs with 3<=n<=10. Finally, the most critical vertex in a Birnbaum-type sense may depend on the failure probability: a six-vertex graph, of smallest possible order, changes leader once, at $p^*=3-\sqrt5$. Adding universal vertices lifts the budget-one examples to every fixed budget, so over all connected graphs the same constants are optimal at every fixed budget; behaviour within restricted classes such as trees is left open.

item.title: Flip-packability: uniform characterisations of tame graph classes
item.description: A class of graphs is monadically dependent if one cannot encode all graphs in coloured graphs from the class using a fixed first-order formula, and monadically stable if one cannot even encode arbitrarily long linear orders. Bonnet et al. (ICALP 2025) characterised monadic dependence by flip-separability: for every vertex weighting, boundedly many flips - complementations of the adjacency relation within a vertex subset - make every ball of radius $r$ carry at most an $\varepsilon$-fraction of the weight, so that every set carrying an $\varepsilon$-fraction has two elements pulled apart. We introduce flip-packability: boundedly many graphs, each obtained from the input by boundedly many flips and all determined by the weighting before any set is presented, such that every set carrying an $\varepsilon$-fraction of the weight has $m$ elements pairwise far apart in one of them. The number of flips producing each graph depends on the radius alone; only the number of graphs depends on $\varepsilon$ and $m$.
